title: Imaging Equipment and Image Production
description: X-ray generators and circuits, the X-ray tube and its ratings, grids and beam-limiting devices, fluoroscopy, and digital image processing.

topics.title: X-ray Generators and Circuits
topics.summary: Transformers, rectification, generator types, and the exposure timer.

notes.b: An X-ray generator supplies high voltage (kV) to the tube and low-voltage current to heat the filament. The autotransformer allows kVp selection; the high-tension (step-up) transformer produces tens of kilovolts; the filament (step-down) transformer heats the filament to control tube current (mA). Rectification converts AC to DC so that electrons always flow from cathode to anode: single-phase generators produce a pulsating waveform with 100% ripple; three-phase generators (6- or 12-pulse) reduce ripple (about 13% and 4%); modern high-frequency (medium/high-frequency inverter) generators produce nearly constant potential (< 1% ripple), giving more efficient, higher-energy output with shorter exposures and smaller units.

Exposure timers terminate the exposure; automatic exposure control (AEC) uses ionisation chambers between the patient and receptor to end the exposure when enough radiation has reached the receptor, giving consistent image density. Correct patient centring over the selected AEC chamber is essential; for example, centring a chamber over a dense area or a prosthesis prolongs exposure. Falling-load generators start at maximum mA and reduce it to keep within tube ratings, shortening exposure times.
k: AEC: ionisation chambers end the exposure

topics.title: The X-ray Tube and Tube Ratings
topics.summary: Rotating anode design, focal spots, heat units, tube rating charts and tube care.

notes.b: The X-ray tube insert is an evacuated glass or metal envelope containing the cathode (tungsten filament(s) in a focusing cup — dual filaments give broad and fine focus) and the anode. Rotating anodes (tungsten–rhenium target on a molybdenum/graphite disc, rotating at about 3,000–10,000 rpm) spread heat over a large focal track. The anode angle (typically 7–17°) sets the effective focal spot via the line-focus principle — smaller angles give smaller effective focal spots but more heel effect and limited field coverage. The tube housing is lead-lined, oil-filled for cooling and insulation, and limits leakage radiation. The tube window lets the useful beam out.
k: Dual filament: broad and fine focus

notes.b: Heat is the main limiting factor. Heat units (single-phase) = kVp × mA × seconds (multiplied by about 1.35 for three-phase, 1.4 for high-frequency). Tube rating charts show the maximum safe combinations of kVp, mA and time for single exposures; anode cooling charts and housing cooling charts guide series of exposures. Good practice: warm up the tube with low exposures after it has been idle (to avoid cracking a cold anode); avoid holding the 'prep' button unnecessarily (filament evaporation deposits tungsten on the envelope, causing arcing); use the lowest mA and broad focus when fine detail is not needed; and respect cooling times. Tube failure causes include filament burnout, anode pitting/cracking and bearing wear.
k: Heat units = kVp × mA × s (× correction)

topics.title: Grids, Beam Restriction and Scatter Control
topics.summary: Collimators, grid ratio and frequency, grid types, grid errors and the air-gap technique.

notes.b: Beam-limiting devices (light-beam diaphragm/collimator, cones and cylinders, aperture diaphragms) restrict the field to the area of interest, reducing patient dose and scatter production (which improves contrast). Scatter increases with field size, patient thickness and kVp.
k: Scatter ↑ with field size, thickness and kVp

notes.b: Anti-scatter grids are strips of lead separated by radiolucent interspace material, placed between patient and receptor to absorb obliquely travelling scatter. Grid ratio = height of lead strips ÷ interspace width (e.g. 8:1, 10:1, 12:1); higher ratios remove more scatter but need more exposure (Bucky factor) and more precise alignment. Grid frequency is lines per cm. Types: parallel, focused (strips angled to converge at a focal distance), crossed, stationary and moving (Potter–Bucky — reciprocating to blur grid lines). Grid cut-off (loss of density) results from off-centre, off-level, off-focus (wrong SID) or upside-down focused grids. Grids are generally used for body parts thicker than about 10–12 cm or above about 60–70 kVp. The air-gap technique (increasing object–image distance) reduces scatter without a grid, but increases magnification.
k: Higher ratio: better clean-up, more dose

topics.title: Fluoroscopy
topics.summary: Image intensifiers and flat-panel detectors, automatic brightness control, and dose-saving features.

notes.b: Fluoroscopy provides real-time moving images for barium studies, interventional procedures, orthopaedic theatre (C-arms) and catheter placement. Traditional image intensifiers convert X-rays to light (caesium iodide input phosphor), then to electrons (photocathode), which are accelerated and focused onto a small output phosphor — brightness gain = minification gain × flux gain. Magnification modes use a smaller part of the input phosphor, improving resolution but increasing patient dose. Modern systems use flat-panel detectors, which avoid geometric distortion (pincushion) and veiling glare. Automatic brightness control (ABC) adjusts kVp and mA to maintain image brightness as patient thickness changes.

Fluoroscopy can deliver high skin doses; deterministic skin injury is possible in long interventional procedures. Dose reduction: minimise screening time (a 5-minute audible alarm reminds operators), use pulsed fluoroscopy at low frame rates, last-image hold, collimation, keep the tube as far and the detector as close to the patient as practical, avoid unnecessary magnification, rotate the beam angle in long procedures to spread skin dose, and record dose–area product (DAP) and fluoroscopy time. Staff wear lead aprons, thyroid shields and lead glasses, and use ceiling-suspended screens.

topics.title: Digital Image Processing and Display
topics.summary: Pixels and matrices, bit depth, windowing, exposure indices, processing and display monitors.

notes.b: A digital image is a matrix of pixels; each pixel's value represents the signal (grey level). Spatial resolution depends on pixel size and matrix (e.g. 2,048 × 2,048); contrast resolution depends on bit depth (a 12-bit image has 2¹² = 4,096 grey levels; 14-bit has 16,384). Digital detectors have a wide dynamic range and linear response, so over-exposure may not look 'too dark' — this can lead to 'dose creep'. Exposure indices (EI, with target EI and deviation index DI) indicate whether the detector received appropriate exposure.
k: Pixel matrix and pixel size → spatial resolution
Wide dynamic range → dose creep risk

notes.b: Post-processing includes look-up tables (LUTs) applied according to anatomical region, windowing (window width controls contrast — a narrow window gives high contrast; window level/centre controls brightness), edge enhancement, noise reduction, and stitching. Processing errors can create artefacts (e.g. halo around metal with excessive edge enhancement, incorrect histogram analysis when collimation is not recognised). Images are viewed on calibrated diagnostic monitors (DICOM Grayscale Standard Display Function) under suitable ambient lighting, and are stored in PACS. Data protection and correct patient identification are essential.
